speaker: David Vélez
title: How He Built the World’s Largest Digital Bank with 140 Million Customers | David Vélez
question: In consumer lending, can a financial institution actively create creditworthiness for unbanked borrowers rather than only measuring it?
guest: Yes, absolutely. First you have to record transactions into a digital ledger, which moving away from cash enables. Then with better algorithms and better product design, you can help people actually build a credit history. We were the first credit card for 30 million people in Latin America. When we asked incumbent banks why they did not extend credit, they said people did not want credit cards or were afraid of taxes. What was really missing was a product matched to their needs. So we started many customers with a twenty-dollar credit line. Traditional banks thought that looked absurd, but customers appreciated that twenty dollars was better than zero—and over time twenty became a hundred, and a hundred became a thousand. You enable them to create a credit history through the right starter product, and then you pair that with an AI copilot coaching them on spending, saving, and repayment moves to improve their creditworthiness.

points.core: Unbanked consumers often lack appropriately sized starter products rather than credit demand.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Yes. Creditworthiness is not a fixed trait waiting to be discovered; it is partly a product of the lending relationship itself, and lenders can build it deliberately.

The most common mechanism is progressive lending: start with a very small loan, observe repayment, and raise limits step by step. This generates a repayment history where none existed, and the prospect of larger future loans gives the borrower a reason to repay. Microfinance institutions such as Grameen pioneered this, and mobile lenders like M-Shwari in Kenya scaled it.

Other tools work similarly. Credit-builder loans and secured cards lock funds in savings while reporting payments to bureaus, manufacturing a credit file. Group lending substitutes social collateral for financial collateral. Bundling loans with savings accounts, financial coaching, payment reminders, and flexible repayment schedules improves the borrower's actual capacity and habits, not just the lender's information.

Evidence is mixed on magnitude. Credit-builder products help people without existing debt most, and can hurt those already struggling. Aggressive digital microlending has also left many borrowers blacklisted, so design matters: creation works when loan sizes, pricing, and reporting are calibrated to borrower success.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Yes. Creditworthiness is not purely an innate borrower trait waiting to be measured; it is partly shaped by how financial products are designed and managed.

First, institutions build formal visibility where none existed. Through credit-builder loans, secured cards, and the reporting of rent, utility, or mobile-money payments, lenders help unbanked borrowers translate everyday reliability into bureau-recognized track records.

More fundamentally, lenders can cultivate actual repayment capacity and behavior. Progressive lending—starting with small, low-risk loans where on-time repayment unlocks larger limits and lower rates—creates strong dynamic incentives for financial discipline. Aligning due dates with irregular cash flows, pairing credit with automated savings buffers or timely reminders, and providing affordable short-term liquidity also help borrowers weather income shocks without turning to predatory informal debt, directly lowering default risk.

There are clear limits: product design cannot overcome severe, chronic income deficits, and poorly structured, high-cost loans can easily destroy creditworthiness through over-indebtedness. Still, thoughtful entry-level lending genuinely co-creates creditworthy borrowers rather than merely discovering them.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Yes. Creditworthiness isn't a fixed trait waiting to be measured. It depends partly on the loan's design, the incentives it creates, and whether the borrower gets a chance to build a record. A lender can therefore help produce it.

Several approaches do this. Microfinance lenders like Grameen use progressive lending: they start with small loans and increase them after each on-time repayment. The promise of future access gives borrowers a reason to repay, and each repayment adds to their record. Credit-builder loans and secured cards report on-time payments to credit bureaus, which creates a credit file where none existed. Lenders can also lower default risk through how they structure loans, using flexible repayment schedules, group liability, automatic payments, or payments timed to when income arrives. Alternative data such as rent, utility and mobile payments can make existing reliability visible.

The effects are real but uneven. In a randomized trial, Burke, Jamison, Karlan, Mihaly and Zinman found that credit-builder loans raised scores for people with no existing debt. They could lower scores for people already carrying loans, who sometimes missed payments. So a lender can create creditworthiness, but only by matching the product to the borrower and accepting early losses.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Yes, financial institutions can actively cultivate creditworthiness rather than merely measuring it, though within real economic limits. Traditional underwriting treats creditworthiness as a fixed trait to be discovered, which excludes unbanked borrowers who lack formal records. In contrast, lenders can build both observable credit profiles and stronger repayment capacity through deliberate product design. Credit-builder loans, secured cards, and graduated microloans start borrowers with low-risk commitments that establish bureau-reported payment histories while accumulating savings buffers. Institutions can also formalize existing financial discipline by integrating rent, utility, or mobile-money payments into credit reporting, turning informal reliability into portable credentials. Beyond record-building, behavioral scaffolding—such as automated mobile-wallet deductions, payment reminders, flexible schedules aligned with irregular income, and bundled savings—actively improves repayment outcomes. Still, lenders cannot manufacture income out of thin air. Creating creditworthiness works when it unlocks latent reliability and strengthens financial habits, not when it extends debt beyond a household's genuine ability to repay.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Yes. A lender can help an unbanked borrower build a record of repayment and strengthen their ability to repay. For example, it can offer a low-cost credit-builder loan with installments the borrower can afford and report payments to credit bureaus. A credit-builder loan that releases the funds after repayment can also help the borrower build a savings cushion. A CFPB evaluation found that borrowers without existing debt were more likely to benefit from these loans. [CFPB evaluation](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/targeting-credit-builder-loans/)

The distinction matters because a credit score documents repayment behavior, while income, expenses, and savings determine whether the next loan is affordable. A lender can influence both, and an unaffordable starter loan can leave the borrower worse off.

noweb.answer:
Yes. A lender can help unbanked borrowers build both the ability to repay and a record that shows it. For example, it can offer a small, affordable starter loan with payments timed to the borrower’s income and report on-time payments to credit bureaus. A low-cost account with a savings feature can also help borrowers build a cushion for irregular expenses.

Using rent payments or cash-flow data can reveal reliability that a conventional credit file misses. Affordable products can go a step further by helping borrowers improve their financial position and establish a credit history they can use with other lenders. The terms matter because an unaffordable loan can leave a borrower worse off and damage the very credit history it was meant to build.
